lessonTitle: First-Order Response: Time Constant and DC Gain

blocks.text: A DC motor driving a conveyor is switched from rest to a constant 5 V. The speed does not jump: it climbs smoothly, quickly at first and then ever more slowly, until it settles at 120 rad/s. Two numbers describe the entire curve: where it ends up and how long it takes to get most of the way. These are the DC gain and the time constant of a first-order system.

blocks.markdown: A **first-order system** has one energy store (rotor inertia, a thermal mass, a capacitor) and a transfer function of the form $G(s)=\dfrac{K}{\tau s+1}$. Here $K$ is the **DC gain** (output units per input unit, for example rad/s per V) and $\tau$ is the **time constant** in seconds. It corresponds to the differential equation $\tau\dot y+y=Ku$. We assume the system is linear, time-invariant and starts at rest.

blocks.title: Time constant and DC gain
blocks.text: The DC (steady-state) gain is $K=G(0)$, the ratio of final output to a constant input once transients decay. The time constant $\tau$ is the time for the step response to reach $1-e^{-1}=63.2\%$ of its final value; equivalently $-1/\tau$ is the real pole of $G(s)$, and the tangent to the response at $t=0$ would reach the final value at $t=\tau$.

blocks.markdown: **Step response.** For a step of amplitude $A$ the input transform is $U(s)=A/s$, so $Y(s)=\dfrac{KA}{s(\tau s+1)}=KA\left(\dfrac1s-\dfrac{\tau}{\tau s+1}\right)=KA\left(\dfrac1s-\dfrac{1}{s+1/\tau}\right)$ by partial fractions. Inverting gives the response below. The final value is $y_\infty=KA$ (also from the final-value theorem $\lim_{s\to0}sY(s)=KA$), which depends on $K$ and $A$ only and never on $\tau$.

blocks.caption: Step response of $G(s)=K/(\tau s+1)$ to an input step of height $A$.

blocks.title: Identify the motor from measurements
blocks.prompt: A motor is stepped from 0 to $A=5$ V. The speed settles at 120 rad/s and reaches 75.8 rad/s (63.2% of final) at $t=0.30$ s. Find $K$ and $\tau$, and write $G(s)$.

steps.text: Final value divides by step height to give the DC gain.
Check the 63.2% level: $0.632\times120=75.8$ rad/s, which is reached at 0.30 s, so $\tau=0.30$ s.

blocks.answer: $K=24$ rad/s per V, $\tau=0.30$ s, so $G(s)=24/(0.3s+1)$ with a pole at $s=-3.33$ rad/s.

blocks.caption: Step response of a first-order system in units of the time constant

blocks.markdown: **Time to a given fraction.** Setting $1-e^{-t/\tau}=f$ and solving gives $t_f=-\tau\ln(1-f)$. For the 90% point $t_{90}=\tau\ln10=2.303\tau$ (the 10-90% rise time is $2.2\tau$). The same $\tau$ governs the settling time to 2%, which is about $4\tau$. Notice that $t_f$ does not depend on the step amplitude $A$ or the gain $K$: a first-order system is equally fast for large or small steps, as long as it stays linear.

blocks.title: Speed at a given time and 90% time
blocks.prompt: For the motor above ($K=24$ rad/s per V, $\tau=0.30$ s) find the time to reach 90% of final speed for the 5 V step, and the speed at $t=0.5$ s. Then state the final speed for an 8 V step.

steps.text: Speed at $t=0.5$ s with final value 120 rad/s: $\omega=120(1-e^{-0.5/0.3})$ and $e^{-1.667}=0.1889$.
For an 8 V step the final value scales linearly with the amplitude, $y_\infty=KA=24\times8=192$ rad/s, while $t_{90}$ is unchanged at 0.691 s.

blocks.answer: $t_{90}=0.691$ s, $\omega(0.5\ \text{s})=97.3$ rad/s, and the 8 V step settles at 192 rad/s in the same 0.691 s to 90%.

items: Apply the step of known amplitude $A$ from rest and record the output until it stops changing.
Read the final value $y_\infty$ and compute $K=y_\infty/A$.
Find the time at which the output reaches $0.632\,y_\infty$; that time is $\tau$.
Cross-check using the initial slope ($\tau=y_\infty/\dot y(0)$) or a plot of $\ln(1-y/y_\infty)$ against $t$, which is a straight line of slope $-1/\tau$.

blocks.title: Common slips
blocks.text: The time constant is the time to reach 63.2%, not the time to reach the final value (which is never reached exactly). Do not confuse the pole location $-1/\tau$ (rad/s) with $\tau$ (s). Do not forget to multiply by the step amplitude: the gain $K$ alone is not the steady output unless $A=1$.

blocks.title: Two numbers describe everything
blocks.text: $K$ sets the final value for any constant input and $\tau$ sets how long it takes. A faster system (a larger pole magnitude $1/\tau$) has a smaller time constant and a shorter $t_{90}$, but its steady-state gain is independent of speed.

points: A first-order system $K/(\tau s+1)$ responds to a step $A$ with $y=KA(1-e^{-t/\tau})$.
The DC gain is $K=y_\infty/A$; the steady-state output for a step of height $A$ is $KA$.
The time constant is the time to reach 63.2% of the final value; $t_{90}=2.303\tau$, $t_{95}\approx3\tau$ and 2% settling is about $4\tau$.
Times to reach a given fraction are independent of the step amplitude for a linear system.

questions.stem: A load cell is stepped by a force of 40 N and its output rises to a final value of 8.0 V. The output reaches 5.06 V at $t=0.12$ s. Which pair gives the gain $K$ and time constant $\tau$ of the first-order model?

distractorRationale.b: The gain is right, but the time constant was taken from the 90% level instead of the 63.2% level.
distractorRationale.c: The ratio was inverted: $K$ is output over input, not input over output.
distractorRationale.d: The final output was used as the gain without dividing by the step amplitude.

questions.explanation: The DC gain is final output over step height, $8.0/40=0.2$ V/N. The time constant is the time at which the response reaches 63.2% of its final value, and $0.632\times8.0=5.06$ V, so $\tau=0.12$ s.

questions.stem: A first-order mechanical positioner is given a step input of 2 V. Its output eventually settles at 100 mm, and the initial slope of the output (at $t=0$) is 50 mm/s. Find the time constant in seconds.
questions.explanation: For a first-order system the tangent at $t=0$ reaches the final value at $t=\tau$, because $\dot y(0)=y_\infty/\tau$. So $\tau=100/50=2.0$ s. The step height of 2 V is not needed for $\tau$ (it is needed for the gain $K=50$ mm per V).

questions.stem: A thermocouple in a gas stream behaves as a first-order system with time constant $\tau=0.8$ s. How long does it take to reach 90 percent of the final value after a sudden change in gas temperature? Give the time in seconds.
questions.explanation: The 90% time is $t_{90}=\tau\ln10=0.8\times2.303=1.842$ s. This is independent of the size of the temperature step because the system is linear.

questions.stem: A first-order temperature process has transfer function $G(s)=\dfrac{15}{2s+1}$, with input heater power in kW and output temperature rise in $^\circ$C. The heater power is stepped from 0 to 0.6 kW. Find the steady-state temperature rise in $^\circ$C.
questions.explanation: The DC gain is $G(0)=15$ $^\circ$C per kW, and the step height is 0.6 kW, so the steady-state output is $KA=15\times0.6=9.0$ $^\circ$C. The time constant of 2 s affects how fast it gets there, not the final value.

questions.stem: A first-order system has $K=2.5$ and $\tau=1.5$ s and receives a step of amplitude 4 at $t=0$. What is the output at $t=3$ s?

distractorRationale.a: That is $KA(1-e^{-1})$, which would be the value at $t=\tau=1.5$ s, not 3 s.
distractorRationale.c: That is the 95% level ($t=3\tau$) applied to the wrong time; $t/\tau=2$ here, not 3.
distractorRationale.d: This incorrectly assumes the response is linear in time up to 80% of final.

questions.explanation: The final value is $KA=2.5\times4=10$, and $t/\tau=3/1.5=2$ so the fraction reached is $1-e^{-2}=0.8647$. The output is therefore 8.65, which agrees with the table entry of 86.5% at $t=2\tau$.

questions.stem: The time constant of a first-order system is the time taken for its step response to reach its final value.
questions.explanation: The step response approaches its final value asymptotically and never reaches it exactly. The time constant is the time to reach 63.2% of the final value, and about $4\tau$ is needed to be within 2%.

questions.stem: A first-order system initially at rest has its step input amplitude doubled from $A$ to $2A$. Which statement is correct for the linear model?

options.text: Both the final value and the 90% time double
The final value doubles and the 90% time is unchanged
The final value is unchanged and the 90% time halves
The final value doubles and the 90% time halves

questions.correctOptionText: The final value doubles and the 90% time is unchanged

distractorRationale.a: The 90% time depends on $\tau$ only, so it does not scale with the input.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: $y_\infty=KA$ scales with $A$, while $t_{90}=2.303\tau$ does not depend on $A$.
distractorRationale.c: The final value is proportional to the input amplitude for a linear system.
distractorRationale.d: A larger input does not make a linear system respond faster; $\tau$ is fixed by the system.

questions.explanation: For a linear first-order system $y=KA(1-e^{-t/\tau})$, so doubling $A$ doubles every output value and hence the final value. The time to reach any given fraction of the final value depends only on $\tau$, so $t_{90}$ stays at $2.303\tau$.

questions.stem: A pressure transducer is stepped and its reading takes 4.6 s to reach 90 percent of its final value. Assuming first-order behaviour, what is its time constant?

distractorRationale.b: That is the 90% time itself, not the time constant.
distractorRationale.c: This divides by 4, the factor relating the 2% settling time (not the 90% time) to $\tau$.
distractorRationale.d: This divides by 3, which relates the 95% time to $\tau$ rather than the 90% time.

questions.explanation: The 90% time of a first-order system is $t_{90}=\tau\ln10=2.303\tau$. Hence $\tau=4.6/2.303=2.0$ s, and the 63.2% time is 2.0 s, shorter than the 90% time as expected.

questions.stem: A step of amplitude $A$ is applied to $G(s)=K/(\tau s+1)$ from rest. Derive $y(t)$ using partial fractions and use your result to show (a) the value at $t=\tau$ and (b) the 90% time.
questions.explanation: The derivation uses a standard Laplace pair with the pole at $-1/\tau$. Both quoted results follow directly from the exponential, so the 63.2% and 2.303 values are not extra facts to memorise.

questions.stem: Describe, with the quantities you would measure, two independent graphical ways to find the time constant of a first-order process from a recorded step response, and explain how you would check that the first-order model is adequate.
markingGuide: Reads final value and finds the time at which the response reaches 63.2% of it
Alternatively draws the tangent at $t=0$ and finds where it meets the final value (time equals $\tau$)
Mentions plotting $\ln(1-y/y_\infty)$ versus $t$, a straight line with slope $-1/\tau$
Checks consistency: the two estimates agree, and the plot is straight; curvature or an initial delay indicates higher order or dead time
questions.explanation: Independent estimates guard against reading errors, and the semi-log plot is the most sensitive test of first-order behaviour. A pure first-order response has a non-zero slope at $t=0$, while higher-order responses start with zero slope.
